title: What are the gotchas of `split()` — trailing empty strings are dropped by default (use `split(regex, -1)` to keep them), the argument is a regex (so `.` must be escaped as `\\.`), and splitting an empty string returns a one-element array?
shortTitle: What are the gotchas of String.split — dropped trailing empties, regex argument, and splitting an empty string?

s1_definition.profdef: `String.split` divides a string into an array of substrings around matches of a regular expression. There are three classic gotchas. First, the single-argument form uses an implicit limit of zero, which removes trailing empty strings from the result, so two consecutive delimiters at the end disappear; passing a negative limit such as `split(regex, -1)` keeps every trailing empty field. Second, the first argument is a REGEX, not a literal, so metacharacters like the dot, pipe, and backslash must be escaped, meaning a dot must be written as a backslash-dot pattern, otherwise the dot matches any character and the result is an empty array. Third, splitting an empty string returns a one-element array containing the empty string, not a zero-length array, which surprises code that assumes an empty input yields no tokens.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh feeds a form line into a shredder set to cut at every comma. First surprise: if the line ends with two commas and nothing after, the shredder quietly throws away those trailing empty slips, so a fixed-column form loses its last blank fields unless he tells the shredder to keep them. Second surprise: the shredder does not cut on the exact character you typed; it interprets your instruction as a pattern, so if you say cut at a dot, it reads the dot as "cut everywhere" and mangles the whole line, unless you spell out that you mean a literal dot. Third surprise: if he feeds in a totally blank line, the shredder still hands back one blank slip rather than nothing at all. Knowing these three quirks prevents corrupted transaction records.
s1_definition.oneliner: split drops trailing empties unless you pass a negative limit, its argument is a regex so escape metacharacters, and splitting an empty string gives a one-element array containing the empty string.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `String.split` divides a string into an array of substrings around matches of a regular expression. There are three classic gotchas. First, the single-argument form uses an implicit limit of zero, which removes trailing empty strings from the result, so two consecutive delimiters at the end disappear; passing a negative limit such as `split(regex, -1)` keeps every trailing empty field. Second, the first argument is a REGEX, not a literal, so metacharacters like the dot, pipe, and backslash must be escaped, meaning a dot must be written as a backslash-dot pattern, otherwise the dot matches any character and the result is an empty array. Third, splitting an empty string returns a one-element array containing the empty string, not a zero-length array, which surprises code that assumes an empty input yields no tokens.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh feeds a form line into a shredder set to cut at every comma. First surprise: if the line ends with two commas and nothing after, the shredder quietly throws away those trailing empty slips, so a fixed-column form loses its last blank fields unless he tells the shredder to keep them. Second surprise: the shredder does not cut on the exact character you typed; it interprets your instruction as a pattern, so if you say cut at a dot, it reads the dot as "cut everywhere" and mangles the whole line, unless you spell out that you mean a literal dot. Third surprise: if he feeds in a totally blank line, the shredder still hands back one blank slip rather than nothing at all. Knowing these three quirks prevents corrupted transaction records.

**One line to remember:** split drops trailing empties unless you pass a negative limit, its argument is a regex so escape metacharacters, and splitting an empty string gives a one-element array containing the empty string.

sections.s2_technical:
`split(regex)` is shorthand for `split(regex, 0)`. The limit parameter controls both how many times the pattern is applied and how trailing empty strings are handled. With a limit of zero, the pattern is applied as many times as possible and any trailing empty strings are DISCARDED. So `"a,b,,".split(",")` returns an array of just a and b, because the two empty fields at the end are dropped. This is the single most common split surprise, because a fixed-schema parser then sees fewer columns than expected and either misreads data or throws an array-index error.

With a NEGATIVE limit, the pattern is applied as many times as possible and trailing empty strings are KEPT. So `"a,b,,".split(",", -1)` returns an array of four elements a, b, empty, empty. For parsing delimited data where the position of each field matters, such as a CSV where a trailing empty amount or note is meaningful, you must use the negative limit. With a POSITIVE limit of n, the pattern is applied at most n minus one times, so the array has at most n elements and the final element contains the unsplit remainder, which is handy for splitting a key and value only on the first delimiter, for example `"key=a=b".split("=", 2)` gives key and the remainder a=b.

The second gotcha is that the first argument is a regular expression, not a literal string. Characters that are special in regex include the dot, which matches any character, the pipe, which means alternation, the backslash, parentheses, brackets, braces, the caret, dollar, plus, star, and question mark. So `"192.168.0.1".split(".")` does NOT split on dots; the dot matches every character, every piece is empty, and because trailing empties are dropped you get an empty array. To split on a literal dot you must escape it, writing the regex as a backslash followed by a dot, which in a Java string literal is two backslashes then a dot. Similarly splitting on a pipe needs the pipe escaped. When you want a purely literal delimiter and do not want to think about regex, `java.util.regex.Pattern.quote(delimiter)` wraps the text so every character is treated literally.

The third gotcha is empty input. Splitting an empty string returns an array of length one whose single element is the empty string, not a zero-length array. So `"".split(",")` has length one. Code that loops over the result assuming an empty input produces zero tokens will instead process one empty token, which can create a spurious blank record. You should guard empty input explicitly if zero tokens is the intended meaning.

Several related points matter in practice. Leading empty strings are always kept regardless of the limit, so `",a".split(",")` gives an empty string then a, which asymmetry surprises people who expect symmetry with trailing behavior. A run of delimiters produces empty strings between them. For high-performance hot paths, a precompiled `Pattern.split` avoids recompiling the regex each call. A senior engineer stresses that for real CSV with quoted fields, embedded commas, and escaped quotes, you should not hand-roll split at all but use a proper CSV library, because split cannot handle quoting rules, and that for financial records a single misparse can post a transaction to the wrong field, so the keep-empties negative limit and a literal, escaped delimiter are non-negotiable defaults.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India ingests a pipe-delimited and a dot-containing feed of transactions, and three real parsing incidents map directly onto the three split gotchas.

Problem 1 — a transaction line ended with two empty optional fields, a blank memo and a blank channel, and the default split dropped them, so the parser read fewer columns than the schema and assigned the wrong meaning to each field, posting a transaction with a shifted amount. This is exactly the dropped-trailing-empties gotcha, fixed by the negative limit.

Problem 2 — a feed used a dot inside a version tag and a developer tried to split a value on a dot without escaping it, which matched every character and returned an empty array, crashing the parser. This is exactly the regex-argument gotcha, fixed by escaping the dot or using Pattern.quote.

Problem 3 — an occasional blank line arrived and the parser, assuming an empty line yields zero tokens, instead processed a single empty token and created a spurious empty transaction. This is exactly the empty-string gotcha, fixed by guarding empty input.

The fix uses split with a negative limit for the main record, escapes the dot when splitting a versioned code, and guards empty lines. The code defines an `Account`, a `FeedParserService` with a `parseRecord` method using the negative limit, a `splitVersion` method escaping the dot, and a `tokenizeLine` method that guards empty input. The demo parses a record with trailing empties, a dotted version, and an empty line.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transaction line "TXN-1,SAV2001,45000.00,," with two trailing empty fields; a version string "2.1.0"; and an empty line.

Step 1. The demo first splits the transaction line with the default split and reports the length, which is three, because the two trailing empty fields are silently dropped. This reproduces the production misparse where the schema expected five fields.

Step 2. The parseRecord method splits the same line with a negative limit, which keeps the two trailing empty fields, producing five elements. It validates that there are at least five fields and builds a TxnRecord with the transaction id, account id, amount, and the two possibly-empty memo and channel fields. The record is correct and the columns are aligned.

Step 3. The demo then splits the version "2.1.0" on an unescaped dot. Because the dot is a regex metacharacter matching any character, every position matches, every piece is empty, and since trailing empties are dropped the resulting array has length zero. This reproduces the crash from treating the delimiter as a literal.

Step 4. The splitVersion method splits the same version on an escaped dot, written as a backslash-dot pattern, which matches a literal dot. The result is the three parts 2, 1, and 0, as intended.

Step 5. The tokenizeLine method receives the empty line. It guards the empty input explicitly and returns zero tokens, logging a warning. Without the guard, splitting an empty string would have returned a one-element array containing the empty string, creating a spurious empty record.

Step 6. The demo logs the default-split count, the correctly parsed record, the wrong unescaped-dot length, the correct escaped-dot parts, and the guarded empty-line token count, making all three gotchas concrete.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 18:51:20 [INFO] Parsing feed for SAV2001
2026-10-30 18:51:20 [WARNING] default split count = 3 (drops trailing empties!)
2026-10-30 18:51:20 [INFO] parsed record = TxnRecord{id=TXN-1, acct=SAV2001, amt=45000.00, memo='', channel=''}
2026-10-30 18:51:20 [WARNING] unescaped dot split length = 0 (WRONG)
2026-10-30 18:51:20 [INFO] escaped dot split = [2, 1, 0]
2026-10-30 18:51:20 [WARNING] Empty line — returning zero tokens (guarded).
2026-10-30 18:51:20 [INFO] tokenize empty line -> tokens = 0
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input line: "TXN-1,SAV2001,45000.00,,"
    │
    ├─ split(",")      → [TXN-1, SAV2001, 45000.00]        (3 — empties DROPPED)
    └─ split(",", -1)  → [TXN-1, SAV2001, 45000.00, "", ""] (5 — empties KEPT) ✓
                              │
                              ▼
                      TxnRecord(id, acct, amount, memo="", channel="")

  Input version: "2.1.0"
    ├─ split(".")      → []            (dot = ANY char → all empty → dropped) ✗
    └─ split("\\.")    → [2, 1, 0]     (literal dot) ✓

  Input empty: ""
    ├─ "".split(",")   → [""]          (length 1 — one empty token!)
    └─ guarded         → []            (zero tokens, intended) ✓
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — split() Gotchas ═══

  ┌─ Design Decisions ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Always split(regex, -1) for fixed-schema records: columns stay │
  │     aligned even with trailing empty optional fields.           │
  │  Escape regex metacharacters (\\.) or use Pattern.quote.         │
  │  Guard empty input: split("") → [""], not an empty array.       │
  │  For real quoted CSV, use a CSV library, not split.             │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Limit semantics (as prose) ─────────────────────────────────
  limit 0 (default): max splits, trailing empties DROPPED.
  limit -1 (negative): max splits, trailing empties KEPT.
  limit n>0: at most n-1 splits, last element holds the remainder.
  Leading empties are ALWAYS kept regardless of limit.

  ── Class Diagram ───────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────────┐
  │      FeedParserService       │───────▶│      TxnRecord      │
  │  ──────────────────────────  │ builds │  - txnId            │
  │  + parseRecord(String)       │        │  - amount:BigDecimal│
  │    : TxnRecord (split -1)    │        │  - memo, channel    │
  │  + splitVersion(String):List │        └─────────────────────┘
  │    (escaped dot)             │
  │  + tokenizeLine(String):List │        ┌─────────────────────┐
  │    (empty guard)             │───────▶│       Account       │
  └──────────────────────────────┘        └─────────────────────┘

  ── Call Chain ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. parseRecord(line) → split(",", -1) → 5 fields → TxnRecord
  2. splitVersion("2.1.0") → split("\\.") → [2,1,0]
  3. tokenizeLine("") → guard → [] (zero tokens)

  Contract for parseRecord(line):
    Pre:  line is a comma-delimited record with >= 5 logical fields
    Post: returns TxnRecord; trailing empty memo/channel preserved
    Throws: IllegalArgumentException if fewer than 5 fields
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
String.split divides a string into an array around matches of a regular expression, and it has three classic gotchas I always account for. The first is that the single-argument form uses an implicit limit of zero, which discards trailing empty strings, so a record ending in two empty optional fields comes back with fewer columns than the schema expects. The fix is to pass a negative limit, which keeps every trailing empty field and keeps the columns aligned. A positive limit, by contrast, applies the pattern at most that many times minus one and leaves the remainder in the last element, which is handy for splitting only on the first delimiter.

The second gotcha is that the first argument is a regular expression, not a literal. Characters like the dot, pipe, and backslash are regex metacharacters, so splitting on an unescaped dot actually matches every character, produces all empty pieces, and because trailing empties are dropped returns an empty array. To split on a literal dot I escape it as a backslash-dot pattern, or I wrap the delimiter with Pattern.quote so every character is treated literally.

The third gotcha is empty input. Splitting an empty string returns a one-element array containing the empty string, not a zero-length array, so code that assumes an empty input yields no tokens will instead process one spurious empty token. I guard empty input explicitly when zero tokens is the intended meaning. I also remember that leading empty strings are always kept regardless of the limit, which is an asymmetry with the trailing behavior.

In our transaction feed ingestion at National Bank of India, all three bit us in production. A line ending in two empty optional fields was misparsed by the default split, shifting the amount into the wrong column and posting a bad transaction, which I fixed by always splitting with a negative limit. A versioned code split on an unescaped dot returned an empty array and crashed the parser, which I fixed by escaping the dot. And an occasional blank line created a spurious empty transaction because splitting an empty string returns one empty token, which I fixed with an explicit empty guard. The broader lesson I share is that for real CSV with quoted fields and embedded commas I do not hand-roll split at all, I use a proper CSV library, because for financial records a single misparse can post money to the wrong field.
